# Why reusable footnotes?

`reusable-footnotes` is motivated by a writing pattern that is especially common
in **legal scholarship and legal practice**: bibliographic references are placed
in footnotes close to the proposition they support, rather than being visible
only in a reference list at the end of the document.

A legal brief, opinion, memorandum, article, or book may therefore contain a
sentence such as:

> The constitutional interpretation of a rule depends on the institutional
> context in which it operates.¹

and the footnote on that page contains the bibliographic source itself:

> ¹ BARROSO, Luís Roberto. *Curso de direito constitucional contemporâneo*.
> São Paulo: Saraiva, 2024, p. 185.

The same work may legitimately appear again in a footnote on another page. This
is not necessarily accidental duplication: page footnotes make the source
available where the reader needs it, without requiring constant movement to a
final bibliography.

This citation culture is particularly visible in **Law**, but related practices
are also common in **History, Philosophy, Theology, Classics, literary studies,
and other Humanities disciplines**.

# The central idea

The important distinction is between a **source** and an **occurrence of that
source in the text**.

A source should be defined only once:

```text
barroso2024
    │
    ├── citation occurrence on page 2  → footnote
    ├── citation occurrence on page 7  → footnote
    └── citation occurrence on page 14 → footnote
```

The bibliographic identity is reusable, while each citation occurrence can be
rendered as a footnote at the point where it is needed.

This is a better conceptual model for legal citation than treating the full
bibliographic text itself as something the author must copy and paste repeatedly.

# Current textual-footnote support

Version 0.2.2 still supports ordinary Pandoc/Quarto footnotes. Repeated notes can
be recognized from their AST content.

## Inline notes

The first statement uses an inline note.^[A reusable explanatory note can be
written with the normal Pandoc inline-footnote syntax.]

The same note can occur again later.^[A reusable explanatory note can be written
with the normal Pandoc inline-footnote syntax.]

```markdown
The first statement.^[A reusable explanatory note.]

The later statement.^[A reusable explanatory note.]
```

## Named notes

Named Markdown footnotes also remain valid.[^named]

The same definition can be referenced again.[^named]

[^named]: A named explanatory footnote defined once in the source document.

```markdown
First occurrence.[^named]

Later occurrence.[^named]

[^named]: A named explanatory footnote defined once in the source document.
```

# Why BibTeX should become the source of truth

For **bibliographic** footnotes, comparing repeated prose is not the most
idiomatic solution. Quarto already has a native identity system for references:
**citation keys** backed by BibTeX, BibLaTeX, CSL JSON, or other bibliography
formats.

A bibliography entry such as:

```bibtex
@book{barroso2024,
  author    = {Barroso, Luís Roberto},
  title     = {Curso de direito constitucional contemporâneo},
  publisher = {Saraiva},
  address   = {São Paulo},
  year      = {2024}
}
```

already gives the source a stable identifier: `barroso2024`.

The extension should therefore reuse **that identifier**, rather than asking the
author to repeat the formatted reference text manually.

# Proposed native citation API

> **Design target:** the BibTeX-backed examples in this section describe the
> intended next API. They are not yet the behavior implemented by v0.2.2.

There are two plausible Quarto-native forms.

## Option A — citation syntax creates the footnote

This is the most idiomatic form for a document whose citation system is entirely
footnote-based:

```markdown
The constitutional question has been discussed extensively.[@barroso2024, p. 185]
```

The author writes a normal Quarto citation. A note-style citation renderer turns
that citation into a real footnote.

The desired result is conceptually:

```text
The constitutional question has been discussed extensively.¹

────────────────────────────────────────
¹ BARROSO, Luís Roberto. Curso de direito constitucional contemporâneo.
  São Paulo: Saraiva, 2024, p. 185.
```

A later citation reuses the same BibTeX identity:

```markdown
The same author returns to the institutional problem.[@barroso2024, p. 241]
```

but creates another citation occurrence and therefore another footnote at that
point in the document.

## Option B — an explicit footnote containing a citation

For documents that mix ordinary inline citations and legal-style footnote
citations, standard Pandoc syntax already provides another expressive form:

```markdown
The constitutional question has been discussed extensively.^[@barroso2024, p. 185]
```

This is attractive because both components remain native:

- `^[...]` is a Pandoc footnote;
- `@barroso2024` is a Pandoc/Quarto citation;
- the `.bib` file remains the only bibliographic database.

The extension would only need to change the **rendering mode** of the citation
inside that footnote.

# The important formatting requirement

The goal is **not** to place the normal inline citation form inside a footnote.
For example, this is not the desired result:

```text
¹ (Barroso 2024, 185)
```

Instead, the citation should be rendered in a **long bibliographic form**, close
to the entry that would normally appear in Quarto's final reference list:

```text
¹ BARROSO, Luís Roberto. Curso de direito constitucional contemporâneo.
  São Paulo: Saraiva, 2024, p. 185.
```

This distinction matters because CSL has separate concepts for **citation
layout** and **bibliography layout**. A normal inline citation uses the citation
layout; a final reference list uses the bibliography layout.

For `reusable-footnotes`, we want a citation occurrence to behave like a
footnote while retaining the richer bibliographic representation of its source.

# A promising implementation path

Pandoc exposes the pieces needed for a native implementation:

1. citations remain ordinary `Cite` nodes with BibTeX keys;
2. bibliography entries can be loaded through Pandoc's own bibliography system;
3. a Lua filter can use Pandoc's cite processor instead of parsing BibTeX itself;
4. the rendered long-form entry can then be placed inside a real `Note` node;
5. HTML, PDF, and DOCX writers can render that `Note` natively.

This means the extension does **not** need a second bibliography parser and does
not need Python or output-specific post-processing.

# CSL strategy

There are two implementation strategies worth comparing.

## 1. A bundled full-note CSL style

A CSL style can be configured as a note style whose citation layout uses the
same rich macros as its bibliography layout.

Then the author could simply write:

```markdown
[@barroso2024, p. 185]
```

and Pandoc/citeproc would generate the footnote.

Advantages:

- maximally native Quarto/Pandoc workflow;
- locators such as pages and sections remain handled by CSL;
- repeated citations, abbreviated subsequent citations, and `ibid.` behavior can
  all be controlled declaratively by CSL;
- works naturally across HTML, PDF, and DOCX.

The limitation is that the long footnote form is defined by that CSL style; it
is not automatically the bibliography layout of every arbitrary CSL file.

## 2. Render an individual bibliography entry through citeproc

Pandoc's Lua API provides `pandoc.utils.references()` and
`pandoc.utils.citeproc()`. This makes a more general strategy possible: the
extension can resolve a citation key, ask Pandoc itself to render that reference
as a one-entry bibliography, extract the resulting `csl-entry`, and place that
content in the footnote.

Advantages:

- the long form can closely follow the actual bibliography representation;
- the user's BibTeX database remains authoritative;
- the extension can potentially work with the user's existing CSL instead of
  requiring a dedicated legal citation style.

The harder part is handling citation-specific information such as `p. 185`,
prefixes, suffixes, and sophisticated CSL rules for subsequent citations.

# Recommended first BibTeX milestone

A good first implementation would support:

```markdown
A proposition.^[@barroso2024]

A proposition with a locator.^[@barroso2024, p. 185]

Several authorities.^[@barroso2024; @silva2023]
```

with these rules:

- bibliography data comes from Quarto's normal `bibliography:` metadata;
- citation keys are the reusable identities;
- each occurrence creates a real footnote;
- the default footnote representation is long-form;
- page/section locators are preserved;
- an optional final bibliography can still be generated;
- no bibliography text is duplicated manually in the `.qmd` source;
- the implementation remains Lua + Pandoc/Quarto only.

Later modes could add:

- `full`: full reference at every occurrence;
- `short`: full first citation, shortened subsequent citations;
- `ibid`: traditional `ibid.` behavior when appropriate;
- a legal-specific bundled CSL profile;
- user-provided footnote CSL styles.

# Why this is still "reusable-footnotes"

The reusable object is not necessarily the rendered footnote number. For legal
bibliographic writing, the reusable object is the **reference definition**.

BibTeX defines the source once; each `@key` occurrence instantiates that source
as a footnote where the argument needs documentary support.

That model is both closer to legal writing practice and more idiomatic in
Quarto than copying formatted bibliographic prose into repeated `^[...]`
expressions.

# Current output behavior

For the existing textual-footnote implementation:

| Format | Repeated textual note |
|---|---|
| HTML | Reuses the canonical note within the rendered page |
| PDF | Reuses the canonical note with clickable repeated markers |
| DOCX | Reuses the canonical note within the configured DOCX scope |

The proposed BibTeX mode is intentionally different: **each bibliographic
citation occurrence should normally become a real footnote**, while the
bibliographic source definition itself remains reusable through its citation
key.
